item.title: A question for teachers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“A man without an aim is like a ship without a radar.” Almost each and every one of us has written this line at some point in our academic life, usually in a paragraph or an essay titled “Aim in life.”
There is nothing wrong with the sentence. A person should certainly have a direction in life. But the real problem came afterwards.
Why did our ships become the same? Why did they all sail towards the same destination? Can everyone’s aim in life really be the same? Perhaps this is where the failure began, passing from one generation to another.
From class 6 or so, we started writing about our aim in life. In Bangladesh, we traditionally followed specific grammar and composition books, guidebooks, and teachers’ notes. Teachers often provided model answers and encouraged students to follow them because those answers were considered safe for examinations and could help students get good marks.
What were we actually writing?
If I am not wrong, there were usually three popular aims in life: Doctor, engineer, and teacher. We did not have to think too much. The professions were already available. We only had to choose one and memorize the paragraph.
The doctor would return to his native village and provide free medical treatment to poor people.
The engineer would contribute to the development of the country.
The teacher would educate the nation and build the future generation.
The stories were almost identical. Only the handwriting was different.
Having some experience in school teaching, I have seen the most ironic part of it. A student from a commerce background is still writing: “I want to become a doctor.”
Does the student genuinely want to become a doctor? Probably not. Because that is what the student has been taught to write in the exam.
Why is this problematic?
The whole idea becomes problematic when we ask children to decide their future by memorizing a model answer.
Why should everyone become a doctor and then go back to their native village to provide free medical service? How would they earn a living? How would they build a career?
And if everyone became a doctor, engineer, or teacher, who would become the banker, entrepreneur, journalist, farmer, designer, or researcher?
We never discussed these questions. The purpose was to write something that would satisfy the examiner.
And then comes the bigger question: How many of us actually reached the destination we wrote about? How many of those students became doctors and engineers? What happened to the rest?
Perhaps the student who wrote, “I want to become a doctor,” eventually became a teacher. Another became an artist, a businessman, a journalist, or a photographer. Someone started a restaurant. Someone left the country. Someone became a parent and devoted his or her life to raising a family.
Did they fail? Of course not. They simply discovered their passion or a different destination.
And this is where I want to ask our teachers a question. What if a student today writes, “I want to become a YouTuber or an influencer”? What if they write “chef”, “singer”, “cricketer”, “footballer”, “content creator”, “gamer”, or “entrepreneur?”
Would you immediately consider these answers less respectable than “doctor” or “engineer?”
Perhaps some teachers would say that children need realistic ambitions. Some may argue that social media careers are uncertain and that students should focus on traditional professions.
There is certainly a valid concern here. Not every ambition will become a sustainable career, and students need guidance about the realities of different professions.
But guidance and imposition are not the same thing. A teacher’s responsibility should not be to tell every student where the ship must go. It should be to teach the student how to navigate, read the map, understand the risks, and choose a destination.
The world has changed dramatically since many of us were students. New professions have emerged. The way people work has changed.
A young person can now earn a living through skills that did not even exist as recognized professions some years earlier.
Yet our classrooms sometimes continue to operate with the same old list of acceptable dreams.
Perhaps it is time to change the answer. Perhaps it is also time to change the way we evaluate the answer.
A student does not necessarily have to write what we expect to see.
Maybe the problem is not that students have the wrong dreams. Maybe we have been evaluating their dreams with the wrong expectations.
Maybe we should be more interested in understanding why a student has chosen a particular goal.
It should be a student’s own answer to a very difficult question: “What do I want to do with my life?”
Md Inzamul Haque is a lecturer at the Department of English, Southeast University. He can be reached at inzamul.haque@seu.edu.bd .

item.title: Helping teachers teach. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Today, we observe World Teachers’ Day under Unesco’s global call to value teacher voices and transform education. For Bangladesh, this day must be looked at as a moment of collective reflection when it comes to education, and how we support educators across all levels.
Any education system is only as strong as its educators. Yet for decades, our classrooms have suffered from chronic underfunding, politicization, and systemic administrative neglect.
If we are to build an equitable, knowledge-driven society, empowering and supporting our teachers must become the bedrock of national policy.
This starts with having an adequate budget for the sector as a whole, something we have struggled with as a nation.
When yearly budgets allocate insufficient funds for education, it signals to the rest of the country that it is a sector not worth investing in, despite the lofty claims of it being the backbone of a nation. The present government has rightfully been commended for increasing the allocation, but having more money is only the first step.
For teachers, the lack of continuous, high-quality pedagogical training and modern digital tools also remain barriers, and it is students who suffer as a result.
Furthermore, the persistent practice of politicizing teacher recruitment, promotions, and school governing bodies has eroded academic meritocracy, discouraging passionate talent from entering the profession.
Rote learning, outdated syllabi, and severe disparities in learning outcomes between urban and rural areas continue to leave millions of students unprepared for the demands of a globalized economy, and it is good teachers who will be able to begin fixing these deep-rooted issues.
Restoring the integrity of our education system requires treating teachers not as administrative instruments but as essential architects of our nation’s future.
As such, instituting comprehensive structural reforms and ensuring the continuous investment in our educators is among the most vital investments in our nation’s potential. Let this day serve as a firm commitment to give our teachers the dignity, resources, and respect they truly deserve.

item.title: Rethinking urban living. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With October 5 being recognized as World Habitat Day, and under the United Nations theme "Adequate Housing for All," Bangladesh must face its inescapable urban crisis.
In a rapidly urbanizing nation where millions of people reside in informal settlements in our major cities, the right to adequate shelter remains a distant promise for a vast segment of our population.
Housing is not merely a roof overhead but encompasses basic sanitation, clean drinking water, and safety. For millions of low-income families, the absence of these basic conditions represents a daily struggle for human dignity.
Our urban planning apparatus has long suffered from a deep structural imbalance. While high-end residential real estate and luxury high-rises dominate development plans, affordable housing for the working poor receives little more than token budgetary allocations.
This disparity is compounded by sprawling slum settlements prone to frequent fires and severe vulnerability to seasonal natural disasters. Given the impact of climate change, flooding and erosion displace rural households daily and our major cities are forced to absorb thousands of new arrivals without the infrastructure to house them safely.
Addressing this deficit therefore will require moving past ad-hoc interventions. The state must treat housing as a fundamental social right and a public good.
Delivering "adequate housing for all" demands integrated and planned urban development -- including low-cost public housing projects, long-term rental assistance, slum-upgrading initiatives, and decentralized urban planning to ease pressure on the capital and other major cities.
Urban sustainability cannot be achieved while millions remain functionally unhoused or trapped in hazardous living environments. We need the authorities concerned to enact inclusive housing policies that prioritize marginalized populations.
Ensuring safe, dignified, and climate-resilient shelter for every citizen is not an impossible ideal but a prerequisite for a stable, equitable, and humane nation.

item.title: Rethinking public sector management and governance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The existing career planning wing of the Ministry of Public Administration performs an important administrative role, but it should not be expected to substitute for a dedicated research-oriented mechanism with a broader mandate for evidence-based human-resource policy.
The HRRC could also study patterns of posting, transfer, promotion, disciplinary action, training opportunities, and leadership selection to identify systemic weaknesses and develop objective policy recommendations.
Such a mechanism could help ensure that individual professional experiences are transformed into institutional learning rather than remaining isolated personal stories.
From administrative control to results-based governance
Public-sector management should ultimately be measured by outcomes.
Citizens do not experience government through organizational charts or administrative procedures. They experience government through the services they receive, the fairness of public institutions, the accessibility of government programmes, and the responsiveness of officials.
Therefore, public-sector reform should increasingly emphasise:
Inputs → Processes → Outputs → Outcomes → Public Value
This requires stronger performance management, better coordination, effective use of data, digital transformation, institutional accountability, and continuous evaluation.
The objective should be to move from a culture of procedural compliance alone towards a culture of results, responsiveness, and public value.
My experience in managing development projects also demonstrated that safeguarding public resources is an essential component of results-based governance.
While serving as additional secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, I also served, in addition to my regular responsibilities, as project director of the CECCR project, now associated with the development of the National Institute of Environment and Climate Change (NIECC).
During my tenure, an endowment fund accumulated under the project attracted attention from senior quarters. I took the position that the funds could not be utilized except in accordance with applicable rules and for their intended institutional purpose.
Subsequently, I was withdrawn from the project before its completion and another officer was assigned responsibility. From my professional perspective, this was an unusual development because project directors would ordinarily continue until project completion, the end of their tenure, or a legitimate public-interest requirement for reassignment.
Nevertheless, I continued to regard the protection of the public interest as the overriding consideration.
An important outcome of that period was the mobilization of approximately Tk10 crore from the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust (BCCT) in accordance with the applicable procedures and the preservation of the funds through fixed deposits with Agrani Bank at the relevant time.
The subsequent institutional evolution of CECCR (currently NIECC), provides an important example of why public resources must be protected even when such decisions may be inconvenient to powerful interests.
Results-based governance is not simply about completing projects. It is also about ensuring that public resources remain protected, traceable, and available for their intended institutional purpose.
Citizen-centred governance
Good governance ultimately depends upon the relationship between the state and its citizens.
Citizens need institutions that are accessible, predictable, transparent, fair, and responsive.
Citizen-centred governance therefore requires public agencies to understand citizens’ needs and evaluate service delivery from the perspective of users rather than solely from the perspective of administrative procedures.
This includes reducing unnecessary administrative burdens, strengthening grievance-redress mechanisms, improving digital services, ensuring equitable access, and making public institutions more responsive to vulnerable and marginalised communities.
Effective field administration requires not merely issuing administrative orders but understanding local realities, responding to grievances, coordinating government agencies, and ensuring that public programs reach intended beneficiaries.
Such reforms can strengthen citizens’ trust in government and reinforce the legitimacy of public institutions.
Public financial management and institutional accountability
Strong public-sector management also requires responsible management of public resources.
Public financial management should be closely connected with governance objectives through:
During my tenure as MD of Jiban Bima Corporation, I sought to strengthen governance in the areas of financial management, administration, business development, and streamlined service delivery.
At one stage, however, serious concerns arose regarding an actuarial valuation undertaken in connection with the Bangladesh Insurance Sector Development Project (BISDP). An external firm was engaged in the process, and the valuation reportedly generated a liability figure of approximately Tk11,00 crore for Jiban Bima Corporation.
In accordance with the applicable provisions of the Insurance Act, 2010, the JBC liabilities, determined through another agency’s valuation, were not accepted during my tenure. Consequently, I incurred the personal wrath of the FID Secretary and Chairman IDRA. These individuals and certain quarters were to establish an exorbitant liability against the Jiban Bima Corporation through an unlawfully executed actuarial valuation, thereby gradually destroying the state-owned corporation and causing private insurance to flourish.
I therefore considered it essential that any such process involving a state-owned insurance corporation should be conducted strictly in accordance with the applicable legal and regulatory framework, with appropriate institutional authorization and accountability.
There is a broader institutional question here: Can a public-sector manager be expected to protect public resources and uphold regulatory standards if doing so exposes the officer to professional retaliation?
This question deserves serious consideration in any discussion of public-sector governance reform.
The lesson is not that individual officers should confront institutional authority. The lesson is that public institutions should create systems in which legitimate disagreement, professional advice, audit concerns, and regulatory objections can be raised without fear of arbitrary retaliation.
Institutional accountability and the protection of public resources
The experience of public-sector management also demonstrates that accountability must extend beyond the individual officer responsible for a decision.
For example, where government vehicles, fuel, project resources, or other public assets are used outside approved rules, the resulting financial burden ultimately falls upon the public.
During my involvement with project management, I observed concerns regarding the use of project vehicles and associated fuel expenditure. Such matters should be addressed through transparent administrative controls, audit mechanisms, and the oversight of the appropriate steering or governing committees.
The responsibility for ensuring such accountability should not rest solely with an individual project director. The relevant ministry, steering committee, audit authorities, and senior administrative leadership all have roles to play.
Institutional accountability therefore must be systemic rather than selective.
Where rules exist but are inconsistently enforced, institutional credibility is weakened. Where audit objections can be neutralised through informal influence, public financial management becomes vulnerable.
Effective governance therefore requires not only rules, but also credible mechanisms for enforcing those rules.
A reform agenda
A comprehensive public-sector management reform agenda could focus on the following priorities:
1. Strengthen the rule of law and regulatory enforcement
Ensure that laws are applied consistently, fairly, and predictably.
2. Institutionalize merit-based human-resource management
Strengthen objective criteria for recruitment, promotion, posting, and professional development.
3. Strengthen civil service training
Move from predominantly procedural training towards competency-based, continuous professional development.
4. Establish the HRRC
Create an evidence-based institutional mechanism for strategic civil-service human-resource research.
5. Strengthen performance management
Link professional development and institutional accountability to measurable performance and results.
6. Promote ethical and professional leadership
Develop leadership standards that emphasize integrity, competence, accountability, and public service.
7. Protect administrative professionalism
Maintain an appropriate balance between political accountability and professional civil-service neutrality.
8. Establish safeguards against arbitrary personnel actions
Ensure that transfers, postings, promotions, and disciplinary measures are based on transparent institutional criteria rather than informal influence.
9. Strengthen citizen-centred service delivery
Measure public institutions by the quality and accessibility of services delivered to citizens.
10. Promote evidence-based policy-making
Increase the use of administrative data, research, evaluation, and comparative international experience.
11. Strengthen public financial management
Ensure that public resources are protected through effective procurement, internal controls, audit, and transparent financial reporting.
12. Strengthen institutional continuity
Ensure that public-sector institutions remain effective across political and administrative transitions.
Way forward
Bangladesh’s future development will depend not only on economic resources or infrastructure but also on the strength and quality of its public institutions.
The central challenge is therefore to build a public sector that is capable, ethical, meritocratic, accountable, innovative, and citizen-centred.
My own experience over a long career in public administration has convinced me that institutional integrity is tested most severely when lawful professional judgment comes into conflict with powerful interests.
I encountered circumstances in which adherence to rules and public interest was not always consistent with the preferences of influential individuals.
On several occasions, refusing to accommodate what I considered improper requests resulted in pressure, threats, investigations, or transfers.
Yet these experiences reinforced, rather than weakened, my conviction that public officials must remain guided by law, evidence, professional ethics, and the public interest.
Citizens are more likely to respect laws when laws are consistently enforced. Public servants are more likely to perform professionally when institutions reward competence and integrity. Governments are more likely to achieve sustainable development when public institutions possess the capacity to translate policy commitments into measurable outcomes.
A strong state does not depend on powerful individuals. It depends on strong institutions.
Bangladesh therefore needs a public administration capable of combining democratic accountability with professional competence, political responsiveness with administrative integrity, and procedural discipline with results-oriented management.
At the same time, civil servants who act according to law and protect public resources should receive institutional protection. Professional integrity cannot be sustained if officers are expected to act ethically but remain vulnerable to arbitrary retaliation for doing so.
Strengthening public-sector human resources should therefore be at the centre of this transformation. The proposed Human Resources Research Cell could contribute to this agenda by providing the evidence, analysis, and institutional perspective necessary for long-term civil-service reform.
Ultimately, public administration is not simply about managing government offices. It is about managing the institutional capacity through which the state serves its people.
Our ancestors rest in this soil, and one day we too will return to it. The enduring measure of public service should therefore be what institutions we strengthen, what public value we create, what public resources we protect, and what standards of integrity we leave behind.
Building capable, accountable, and trusted public institutions is not merely an administrative objective. It is a foundation for sustainable national development and a lasting obligation to future generations.
Md Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is Former Additional Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration, Bangladesh.

item.title: Is grass really green on the other side?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In tea stalls across Dhaka, scrollable feeds on smartphones, and family dinner tables nationwide, a singular refrain echoes with predictable cadence: "Leaving the country is the only way out."
Faced with persistent domestic headwinds -- sticky inflation squeezing household budgets, job market stagnation, and concerns over personal security -- the instinct to seek greener pastures abroad has morphed from an ambition into a standard reflex.
Yet, as thousands of young professionals, students, and workers pack their hopes into polished suitcases, they confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: The global exit door is closing fast.
For a nation of over 170 million people, leaving is no longer a simple matter of ambition; it has become an intricate, exhausting bottleneck.
The harsh reality is that leaving Bangladesh has become almost as difficult as staying -- raising a fundamental question about how we view our collective future.
The ordeal begins long before anyone reaches an international departure terminal. In Bangladesh, the journey abroad starts in government offices, defined by bureaucratic red tape.
Obtaining basic personal credentials -- a birth certificate, a national ID correction, utility-backed address proofs, and eventually a passport -- often becomes a trial of endurance.
Simple typographical errors on a primary school certificate can initiate months of administrative hurdles.
Citizens navigate multiple desks, enduring lengthy delays and arbitrary verification steps just to secure the legal right to apply for a visa.
Before an applicant ever faces a foreign consular officer, their energy and financial resources are significantly drained by domestic administrative processes.
The credibility gap and visa rejections
Even when documentation is complete, foreign embassies present steep hurdles.
Bangladeshi passport holders face exceptionally high visa rejection rates, even for routine travel or higher education.
This trust deficit has not emerged in a vacuum.
Decades of irregular migration, widespread forgery of bank statements and educational certificates by predatory middlemen, and a tendency for individuals to overstay visitor or student visas to seek asylum have damaged the country's international standing.
International immigration authorities now scrutinize applications from Bangladesh with heightened skepticism.
As a result, ordinary students and legitimate professionals pay the price for systemic abuses.
Work visas across traditional labour destinations in the Middle East and Southeast Asia face periodic freezes, while Western nations tighten student intake quotas and financial proof requirements.
The green passport -- frequently ranked near the bottom of global mobility indexes -- reflects a serious credibility issue that limits legitimate opportunities.
Competitiveness gap
Beyond administrative barriers lies a deeper structural issue: Market readiness.
Modern global labour markets demand high specialization, research literacy, fluent communication, and rapid technical adaptation.
In these areas, Bangladesh struggles with persistent gaps.
While neighbouring nations in South Asia have systematically aligned their primary, vocational, and tertiary education systems with global standards, Bangladesh’s educational framework remains fragmented.
Despite years of compulsory English education, many graduates struggle with professional fluency, creating immediate communication barriers during embassy interviews, university applications, and workplace interactions.
Furthermore, tertiary institutions in Bangladesh rarely rank at all in global university lists, leaving graduates at a disadvantage when competing against international peers.
In an era where artificial intelligence and automation are reshaping global workplaces, Bangladeshi jobseekers often lag in leveraging digital tools and AI-driven productivity workflows.
While global candidates use advanced tech stacks to secure remote work or specialized roles, many Bangladeshi applicants remain reliant on traditional skill sets that are rapidly becoming obsolete.
The friction extends beyond skills to international perceptions.
Due to publicized cases of document fraud and irregular migration routes, foreign governments have implemented stricter border policies.
Consulates that once processed thousands of students and work permits annually have raised financial thresholds, reduced quotas, or relocated their processing centers altogether, requiring applicants to travel to neighbouring countries just for an interview.
This institutional skepticism makes the migration process prohibitively expensive and uncertain, turning what used to be a viable career pathway into an unpredictable gamble.
This reality creates a challenging dilemma for young Bangladeshis.
At home, economic pressures are real: High inflation erodes purchasing power, job creation struggles to keep pace with university output, and social security challenges persist.
Yet the alternative abroad is rarely the seamless transition depicted on social media.
Immigrants frequently encounter skyrocketing costs of living, tight housing markets, strict work-hour caps for students, and the constant strain of maintaining legal status.
The realization that life abroad carries its own severe challenges can be discouraging for those who view migration as a guaranteed solution.
Redefining the horizon
While these obstacles may seem daunting, recognizing them offers an important opportunity for recalibration.
The realization that leaving is not a universal solution forces a shift in focus back to building strength from within.
Bangladesh’s greatest asset remains its demographic dividend -- a young, resilient, and adaptive population.
If the path outward is restricted, the imperative shifts to building capacity domestically. This recalibration is already taking shape across several sectors:
The current mobility challenge does not signal the end of progress for Bangladesh's youth.
Rather, it marks the end of a reliance on simple exit strategies.
By shifting focus from escaping domestic challenges to developing competitive skills and improving local systems, the nation can build a context where staying is no longer seen as a compromise, but as a meaningful, viable choice.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Leave small businesses alone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There's a good argument that every business in the country should be registered -- so that we know who is doing what, who is obeying tax laws, and so on.
There's also a good argument for keeping really small businesses completely out of the bureaucratic system -- for really small businesses simply do not have the time, or often even the knowledge, to be able to deal with the bureaucracy.
As is obvious, these two arguments are in conflict with each other.
The correct error -- or at least I would insist, which is not quite the same thing as insisting I am correct to do so -- is to be on the side of allowing small businesses to escape the bureaucracy.
This is the background to the requirement that every business must now have a BIN -- a Business Identification Number.
The claim is that this requirement hits cottage, micro, small, and medium enterprises (CMSMEs) hard. It isn't that applying for the number is difficult. It's that it can be difficult to get the supporting documentation required to be able to make that application.
For example, a legal rental agreement -- or property deed - is required for the business address. Yet plenty of micro businesses run from the left hand side of the family dining table.
If we're talking about manufacturing, then it requires a machinery list, an equipment layout plan, and input-output coefficient information. There are people out there running perfectly fine businesses who don't know what that last part means, and I'm not sure I do either.
It's obvious what is happening here. The bureaucracy thinks it would be a fine thing if everyone in business were doing business correctly and in a formal and registered manner.
Thus they can use the need for a BIN to make sure that everyone is indeed doing things correctly -- working at a property licensed to run a business from, for example. For larger businesses, this could even be true too.
For smaller businesses -- micro, cottage, and so on -- these requirements can be the difference between it being worth being a legal business at all or remaining in the shadows of the grey economy.
Grey here meaning not illegal as a business -- that's the black economy. Just one that's not registered and paying taxes and such.
And here's the thing. We all want to have economic growth. That's how to climb that ladder from a less developed economy all the way up to a developed and rich one.
Economic growth comes from new business formation. Very little of total economic growth comes from large companies growing yet more.
Nearly all of it comes from someone using that corner of the kitchen table to come up with a new idea and trying it out.
Barriers to those tryouts limit, slow, or even stop, economic growth.
The correct answer, therefore, is to reverse that process of applying for the legality of the business.
Get people signed up for the BIN first. Say, if you have some form of personal ID, then you can apply online for that BIN.
Great, you're now a business and you can use that number to gain access to a bank account and all the rest.
We can worry about obeying all of the other laws -- when you need to provide a machinery layout plan, for example -- to when you're a large enough business that it's worth worrying about.
Yes, some people will abuse this reversal of the current process. But that's just the same argument as we started with.
It would be good if everyone was running every business according to all the rules. But the rules also prevent some people from starting up in business at all.
The error should be, again to my mind, on getting the business happening first -- for that's the part that makes us richer -- and worrying about compliance with all the bureaucratic laws later.
Adam Smith pointed out that the only things required to move from barbarism to the highest degree of opulence is peace, easy taxes, and the tolerable administration of justice.
That “tolerable” there means yes, of course everyone absolutely must obey the really important laws but a certain benign neglect of the details is also necessary.
Or even, as we can and should put it, less bureaucracy means more business. Let's err on the side of more business as that's the one that makes us richer.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at Adam Smith.

item.title: Your phone number is now your identity. Guard it. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A shopkeeper in Mirpur comes home from Friday prayers and sees that his phone has no signal. He blames the network, as most of us would. By the time he gets to a service centre the next morning, his mobile wallet is empty, he's locked out of Facebook, and three of his cousins have received messages from "him" asking for money.
The shopkeeper is invented, but the sequence is a familiar one. And none of it took clever hacking. Whoever did this only needed his number.
It's worth stopping to think about how much a Bangladeshi phone number carries these days. It receives the one-time password for your wallet. It's how you get back into Facebook when you forget your password, how WhatsApp knows it's you, how the courier confirms your parcel.
Banks lean on it more every year. We built one of the most phone-dependent economies anywhere, and somewhere along the way, 11 digits became the key to nearly everything. Nobody planned it. It just happened.
Attackers noticed long before users did. In my years running security work in Silicon Valley, I saw them go after whatever opened the most doors, again and again. Here, that's the SIM.
Most of the time they don't even have to take it, because we hand it over.
Someone calls, says he's from your wallet provider, warns that your account will be suspended, and asks you to read out the code you've just received.
Or a message arrives: Sorry, I sent my code to your number by mistake, could you forward it?
These tricks work because Bangladeshis are, on the whole, helpful people who trust a polite voice.
A real provider will never ask for your PIN or OTP. Not by phone, not by SMS, and not through a relative who says the company told them to.
When a fraudster can't talk the code out of you, he may go after the SIM itself and get a replacement issued in your name.
Biometric SIM registration made that much harder. I worked on those systems, and it was a real step forward that many wealthier countries still haven't taken.
It didn't make it impossible, though. Forged papers, a bribed insider, or a careless recovery process can still get someone through.
What you'd notice is your phone going dead while everyone around you still has signal. Most people wait a day before dealing with that, and a day is more than enough.
Then there are the apps: A cracked game, an "update" someone forwarded on WhatsApp, a free copy of something that normally costs money.
Some of these ask to read your SMS, or to use Android's accessibility features, which were built for people with disabilities and let an app see and tap whatever is on your screen.
Say yes, and the app can read your OTPs as they arrive. You never share anything. It simply watches.
Start with the OTP. Treat it like cash, and don't give it to anyone, including someone who sounds exactly like a family member.
Put a PIN on WhatsApp through their two-step verification settings, which takes about two minutes.
If your signal drops for no obvious reason, call your operator from someone else's phone within the hour, and let your wallet provider know too.
Get your apps from the Play Store, and when a torch app asks to read your messages, ask yourself why.
Finally, have one conversation at home about a family code word, something only you would know, to ask for whenever money comes up. It sounds like something out of a movie, but it costs nothing and it works.
Still, it isn't fair to leave all of this to individuals. A phone number was never meant to prove who someone is on its own.
In several countries, banks and mobile operators have started passing each other one simple piece of information: Has this SIM been replaced in the past few days? If it has, the large transfer waits until someone checks.
Bangladesh has already done the hard part with biometric registration, so it could do this more easily than most.
The same thinking applies inside the phone. Security that catches a malicious app before it gets anywhere near a wallet or banking app should come as standard, rather than something people discover after they've been robbed.
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. We tend to measure how digital Bangladesh is by how many people are online. A better measure might be how many of them feel safe once they get there.
Everyone who loses money this way tells their family, their neighbours, the regulars at the tea stall. Each story makes the next person a little warier of going digital, and that wariness takes a long time to wear off.
The number is already our identity. We just haven't started treating it that way.
Zeeshan R Khan led a security practice at Cisco for more than 12 years and is based in Silicon Valley. He is the founder of SurroundApps, which builds mobile security and family-safety technology for Bangladesh.
